title: Fooling LLM Safety Guards into Judging the Wrong Text
description:
arXiv:2610.31695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety guards check content before an LLM application acts on it, and most paste that content into a plain-text prompt. Content that imitates the prompt can append a second task, and the guard answers that one instead. We call this target rebinding. Our explanation is that the guard grades the last complete task in its input, here a harmless decoy, so the harmful request goes through unchanged. In a pre-registered test, an appended forged query and decoy clear all 75 held-out AdvBench requests that Shieldstral-1.0-3B flags. The guard is not persuaded: a directive to ignore the text above clears none of them, and in a follow-up run a harmful decoy stops the attack. On our GuardRebind benchmark, each of five guards has an attack family, chosen per guard, that clears at least 93% of its flagged items. Rebinding explains this best on Shieldstral and gpt-oss-safeguard; on ShieldGemma and Llama Guard 3, generic evasion and trailing text respectively do part of the work, and Qwen3Guard falls mainly to a forgery of its whole task. Training the guard to score content no lower than its most harmful part cuts attack success from 75% to 0.8-1.6% on attack families, decoys and forged queries held out of training. All of these attacks append the forged structure after the request, and we added the held-out-decoy evaluation after a first round of test runs. Clean AUROC falls by at most 0.01, but our test of non-inferiority is inconclusive. A score-guided search still beats this trained guard on 47 of 50 items, usually by placing forged structure before the request. On about half of the items where the search wins, the same search also finds benign text, with no forged structure, that clears the guard.
author: Utkarsh Kanwat

title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
description:
arXiv:2610.31713v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
author: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren

title: SILMARILS-MV: Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signatures with Dealer-Free Key Issuance and Linear Aggregation for Permissioned Blockchains
description:
arXiv:2610.31814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Permissioned blockchains authenticate transactions, votes and quorum certificates with computationally secure signatures, and post-quantum replacements inflate consensus traffic by orders of magnitude. Information-theoretic alternatives have required a trusted authority, quantum channels, per-signature interaction, or single-use keys with bounded transfer. We present SILMARILS-MV, a multi-verifier unconditionally secure signature in which a signature is the vector $\alpha = A\,e(m)$ and each verifier holds a secret functional $c_i = \Gamma^T \lambda(x_i)$ derived from virtual anchors $\Gamma$ that nobody learns. Against unbounded adversaries corrupting up to $\omega$ verifiers and any signers, and observing every decision, an honest verifier accepts a forged or invalid signature with probability at most $Q/q + 1/(q-1)$, a bound that is tight in its leading term. The scheme is strongly unforgeable, non-repudiable, transferable across unboundedly many hops, and linearly aggregatable. Keys are issued by the validators through perfectly secure MPC for $t < n/3$, without broadcast. To scale, we let the committee itself sign: in threshold notarization, finality certificates have constant size $32(\omega+1)$ bytes and per-validator issuance cost no longer depends on $n$. Arbiter-verified keys give clients 32-byte signatures, robust redistribution supports membership changes and share refresh, and verifiers can be enrolled retroactively. A certificate verifies in 2.4 microseconds. In an analytic normal-case model at 1000 validators, threshold notarization needs 71 KiB of authentication traffic per validator per block, 22x less than ML-DSA-44 for admitted verifiers. In a Rust HotStuff prototype with 100 validators, SILMARILS-MV commits 2.8x more transactions per second than ML-DSA-44 with 67x less cryptographic CPU, and Monte-Carlo attacks match the bounds.
author: Khadijeh Bagheri, Hassan Khodaiemehr, Chen Feng

title: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits
description:
arXiv:2610.31831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. However, it is challenging for an LLM to reliably verify its own generated exploits. In this paper, we propose Ulysses, a multi-agent security harness to synthesize verifiable vulnerability exploits for web applications. Ulysses converts candidate vulnerability findings into verified Proofs of Exploitability by iteratively exploring exploit hypotheses and establishing success in independently observed execution effects. We evaluated Ulysses on WebExploitGym, a curated benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications that span 5 languages and 7 frameworks. Ulysses produces verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories. It also discovered 4 new proofs of exploitability that have never been previously reported.
author: Aditya Oke, Andr\'e Vicente Duarte, Rui Melo, Shubham Gandhi, Nachiket Kotalwar, Charmi Khandor, Danqing Wang, Carolyn Ros\'e, Lei Li

title: SEMPRE: Semantic-Aware Protocol Reverse Engineering via Consistency-Driven Joint Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.31844v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Protocol reverse engineering (PRE) is essential for understanding undocumented or proprietary communication formats, enabling security-critical tasks such as vulnerability discovery, malware C2 analysis, and IDS signature generation. However, existing PRE techniques rely on brittle hand-written rules, under-model contextual dependencies among neighboring fields, and often fail on messages with nested sub-protocols. We present SEMPRE, a fully automated PRE framework that replaces ad-hoc heuristics with recursive LLM reasoning grounded in fine-grained dynamic program analysis. SEMPRE uses taint-flow and loop traces to guide an LLM-driven tree-of-thought search that slices messages into fields while detecting nested sub-payloads, producing a hierarchical layout. It then infers each field's type and role and iteratively refines boundaries by freezing high-confidence segments and re-running detection under semantic constraints, yielding an EM-style procedure that monotonically improves structure and semantics until convergence. Evaluated on a broad corpus of mainstream protocols against six state-of-the-art (vs. <0.4 for all baselines) and 0.72 for semantic inference (vs. 0.13 for BinPRE). Ablations confirm the contribution of each component, and a case study on a prolific real-world botnet demonstrates practical utility.
author: Yihua Xu, Weijie Huang, Xiaofeng Wang, Hang Zhang, Binghui Wang, Yue Duan

title: Incomparable Minima in Agent Tool Authorization
description:
arXiv:2610.31914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent that needs a tool needs authority to call it, and every proposal for governing that authority has to answer one question: of two grants that both let the agent finish a task, which one is smaller? Over-privilege benchmarks score agents against this answer, and permission solvers compute it. We check the question against the authorisation tables that Microsoft and Google publish, covering 22,305 Microsoft Graph endpoint bindings and 23,852 Google API methods, on tasks generated from each table's own resource structure. For 29.8-33.3% of Graph tasks and 3.2% of Google resource tasks the question has no answer, because the minimal sufficient grants form an antichain, a set of grants none of which authorises a subset of what another does. In its two main authorisation modes, Microsoft's shipped privilegeLevel rates 67.4-74.4% of these incomparable pairs equal. Google ships no such scale, so on Google we apply a reconstruction of the FORTIS privilege ladder, which rates 90.7-98.7% equal. Applying the same reconstruction to Graph attributes much of that difference to the scale rather than the corpus: its form based on the HTTP verb alone rates 92.0% of Google pairs and 89.0-92.0% of Graph pairs equal. Four risk measures (operations, writes, services reached, administrative surface) order 28.7% of incomparable Google pairs and 15.7-23.4% of Graph pairs in opposite directions, so for those pairs the ranking has no measure-independent answer. Offered pools of minimal and larger grants, 6 frontier models pick a minimal grant on 99.0% of 1,708 decisions, a grant smallest under all four measures on 66.7%, and on 22.1% a grant that another option matches or beats on every measure. We propose that benchmarks report which minimal grant an agent chose and that deployments show the alternatives to whoever approves the grant.
author: Xin Xu

title: Not an Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy in Humanoid Robots
description:
arXiv:2610.31923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As humanoid robots move from research laboratories toward deployment in human-centered environments such as homes, hospitals, and warehouses, safe operation around nearby people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement. Safety filters have emerged as a promising technique to address this challenge by providing mathematical guarantees that generated control actions do not result in collisions.
  This paper shows that these guarantees hold only when the safety parameters are configured correctly. However, correct parameter configurations are task- and environment-specific, and no general method exists to determine them across diverse deployments. As a result, safety filters shipped with humanoid robots can fail after deployment in specific scenarios. We show that attackers can exploit these failures through only normal user interactions without any additional privileges or capabilities. To demonstrate this risk, we present goal insertion attacks and develop SIREN, an automated tool that identifies vulnerable inserting goals for a given task and environment. Experimental results show that SIREN identifies attacks in all vulnerable scenarios in the SPARK dataset. Compared with a baseline approach, SIREN discovers three times as many attacks. We also show that SIREN is able to generate attacks against a real humanoid and cause it to collide while executing tasks. These results demonstrate that current safety filters introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that can cause safety violations, which reveals that existing safety mechanisms can themselves become a source of safety risk for humanoid robots.
author: Tiffany Bao, Shangtao Li, Yifan Sun, Mengwen He, Bowei Li, Alden Wang, Changliu Liu, Ruoyu Wang, David Brumley

title: Agentic AI Defense: Decode-Time Provenance Binding for MCP
description:
arXiv:2610.31974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection through untrusted tool outputs. We demonstrate cross-modal trust laundering, in which instructions concealed in an email-signature image using least-significant-bit (LSB), discrete cosine transform (DCT), or metadata steganography bypass text scanners and enter a multi-agent workflow when decoded by a tool. To counter this threat, we propose decode-time provenance binding, which combines HMAC-authenticated trust labels with an MCP-maintained provenance ledger and context-taint tracking. The mechanism labels decoded content as untrusted and blocks critical tool calls influenced by that content, even when a compromised agent substitutes a valid trusted label. We evaluate the approach using a real MCP testbed with three steganographic carriers and 24 adaptive payloads. The undefended pipeline exhibits 100% attack success, while keyword and regex defenses each permit 62.5% of attacks. Our mechanism blocks all attacks (0% success), including adversarial label substitution across mediated agent boundaries. A four-component ablation validates the roles of decode marking, cryptographic authentication, lineage tracking, and sink enforcement. An audited trusted-promotion mechanism increases legitimate-task completion from 67% to 100% without compromising protection. The approach provides carrier-independent containment within fully mediated MCP execution environments. Code and data are publicly available.
author: Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas, Patrick Tague, Bruce DeBruhl, Yong Wang

title: WADE: An LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection Engine for WebAssembly Applications
description:
arXiv:2610.31984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) enables near-native performance for web applications through a portable and sandboxed execution model. However, its limited runtime protection mechanisms (e.g., the lack of stack canaries and address space layout randomization (ASLR)) leave Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks.
  We present WADE (WebAssembly Anomaly Detection Engine), a system that detects anomalous runtime behaviors in browser-executed WebAssembly applications. WADE monitors function-level execution traces collected under benign conditions and trains a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn the normal execution behavior of each application. At runtime, the model flags deviations from these learned patterns as potential attacks. Unlike signature-based approaches, WADE builds application-specific behavioral models, enabling detection of both known and previously unseen attacks without per-vulnerability signatures.
  We evaluate WADE on a dataset of 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, achieving zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.
author: Ilaria Campestrini, Stefano Zanero, Engin Kirda

title: TRACE: Data-Free Text Reconstruction Attacks against Approximate Unlearning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.31995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) face growing demands for data removal driven by regulatory compliance, copyright concerns, and privacy protection, approximate unlearning has emerged as a practical alternative to expensive full retraining. In practice, pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots are often maintained for auditing and rollback, introducing a previously overlooked side channel. This paper demonstrates that approximate unlearning in LLM can leave residual traces within model snapshots, which may be recoverable and thus enable the privacy breaches that approximate unlearning is intended to prevent. Here, we propose TRACE, a framework that reconstructs unlearned training data given access to pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots, without any data-specific prior knowledge. To achieve this, TRACE identifies a compact set of candidate tokens from embedding-level parameter differences to constrain the search space, and assembles sequences via a contrastive scoring mechanism based on the perplexity gap between the two models. A two-stage exploration-then-completion strategy enables the recovery of multiple distinct samples. Extensive experiments on various datasets, including TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, across multiple LLMs and six representative unlearning methods, demonstrate that TRACE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction. This paper exposes significant privacy risks in current LLM approximate unlearning deployments and highlights the need for defenses against parameter-difference leakage and appropriate management of model snapshot access.
author: Mengying Zhang, Derui Wang, Ibrahim Khalil, Bowen Liu, Xiaoyu Xia, Minhui Xue

title: SynMark: Semantic-Coordinate Multi-Bit Watermarking during LLM Code Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.32017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-generated code is increasingly reused across downstream applications and often undergoes identifier renaming or structural refactoring, making robustness to functionality-preserving edits essential for generative multi-bit code watermarking. Existing methods commonly derive message routes from surface-token prefixes, so such edits can desynchronize routing and degrade watermark recovery. We propose SynMark, which replaces surface-dependent routing with learned semantic coordinates and further calibrates residual recovery errors after transformation. For watermark embedding, Scope learns semantic coordinates from aligned prefixes of functionally equivalent variants for keyed routing and applies a syntax-aware adaptive bias during generation. For watermark extraction, Traced recomputes semantic routes from transformed code and uses reliability-weighted aggregation to suppress unreliable token contributions. Under 100% identifier renaming, SynMark retains 82.27% and 83.77% BitAcc on CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder, respectively. Across three code LMs, it also improves clean BitAcc and Pass@1 by up to 4.53 and 11.18 percentage points over the strongest watermarked baselines.
author: Rui Xu, Weizhi Liu, Zhaoxia Yin

title: SPA: Structure-Preserving Approximation of Gated Activations under FHE
description:
arXiv:2610.32065v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nonlinear activation evaluation remains a major bottleneck in neural inference under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). FHE supports efficient addition and multiplication, but lacks native operations for exponential functions, reciprocals, and value-dependent selection. High-degree polynomial approximations on fixed intervals are therefore commonly used to replace nonlinear activations. They can achieve small errors but often incur substantial multiplicative depth and latency. We observe that several widely used nonlinear activations share the algebraic structure $A(x)=xg(x)$ with $g(-x)=1-g(x)$. This class includes GELU, SiLU, fixed-parameter Swish, and the scalar nonlinear branches of GEGLU/SwiGLU. We propose \SPA{} (\emph{Structure-Preserving Approximation}) to exploit this shared structure. \SPA{} retains the exact odd component $x/2$ and approximates only the even residual as a polynomial in $x^2$, yielding a comparison-free arithmetic kernel. This construction removes redundant odd degrees of freedom and enables lower-cost polynomial evaluation at a given error target. Plaintext experiments with Gemma-4-E2B and Llama-3.2-3B show that SPA largely preserves downstream task performance without weight updates. Fixed-interval CKKS benchmarks show favorable error--latency trade-offs. On $[-5,5]$, \SPA{}-balanced achieves a $3.25\times$ speedup over MOAI (ICLR'~26) for erf-GELU with comparable error. On the same interval, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $79.22\%$ lower root mean squared error (RMSE) and a $10.40\times$ speedup over Euston (S\&P'~26) for QuickGELU. For SiLU, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $19.02\%$ lower RMSE and a $2.06\times$ speedup over THOR (CCS'~25).
author: Rui Li, Wenyuan Wu, Weijie Miao

title: Label-Budgeted Attribute Inference from Protected Features in Edge-Cloud Split Multimodal LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.32079v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Edge-cloud split inference runs the early layers of a multimodal large language model (MLLM) on a device and sends intermediate features to a server to complete the task. While keeping raw images local is often perceived as a privacy benefit, an honest-but-curious server can still infer sensitive attributes, such as age, gender, and race, from the received features. Existing protections intervene at the input, transmitted representation, or model's responses, but their native evaluations rely on final-response refusals or fixed-classifier failures, which underestimate an adaptive server's capabilities. To address this, we propose a label-budgeted attribute-inference framework that measures representation-level privacy through a recovery curve: the share of the unprotected leakage the server recovers as a function of its labeled-sample budget, from zero (a classifier trained on unprotected features) to a full labeled set. Our evaluation across two popular MLLMs reveals two critical findings. First, in unprotected pipelines, intermediate features leak all three attributes regardless of the split depth. Second, even when protection mechanisms are deployed across different stages, sensitive information remains recoverable under limited label budgets. For example, Safe-LLaVA removes biometric content from the model's responses, but from the features it transmits in split inference, 20 labeled samples per class recover 75-85% of the unprotected leakage. This work provides a label-budgeted measure of feature-level privacy for split MLLM inference and motivates defenses that act on the transmitted representation.
author: Junguang Yao, Peichun Hua, Hanxiu Zhang, Yue Zheng

title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.32092v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
author: Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang

title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.32155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities by invoking third-party skills, where each skill encapsulates instructions, scripts, and resources for agents to execute on demand. This paper reveals that deploying many benign skills together introduces compositional security risks: multiple individually clean skills can compose into safety-violation chains, because the agent passes an upstream skill's output to a downstream skill's input across invocations. The risk arises not from any single skill, but from the agent's runtime orchestration, and thus cannot be captured by existing malicious skill detection methods. To this end, we develop KnotScryer to detect insecure skill compositions by treating skills as typed capability flows. In particular, we abstract each skill into a capability summary, and construct the Skill Capability-Flow Graph (SCFG), where edges denote cross-skill information flow. Moreover, we design a search policy that tracks protected or untrusted data along handoff edges to locate paths reaching insecure operations. Finally, a two-layer verification method replays the insecure information flow for reachability analysis and applies a task-anchored LLM chain audit to confirm the semantic plausibility of the identified violation chains. We deploy KnotScryer to analyze 13,598 clean skills from ClawHub, and validate the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. KnotScryer identifies 612 insecure compositions, which are consistently exploited across agent frameworks. Meanwhile, under GLM-5.1, it outperforms tag-match and graph-only baselines by improving the exploitation rate from 16.5%-18.2% to 85.6%, while reducing the search space by 85.3%. Furthermore, 13.7% of the detected chains consist entirely of skills labeled safe by a single-skill scanner, showing that KnotScryer effectively identifies insecure compositions that per-skill auditing cannot.
author: Yihao Li, Chuanpu Fu, Yizhou Zhao, Miao Chen, Qi Li, Ke Xu

title: The 3DS Oracle: BIN Attack via the Network
description:
arXiv:2610.32206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EMV 3-D Secure (3DS) requires a client-visible continuation boundary in browser-mediated flows; in some deployments, that boundary exposes a pre-authorization classification channel. This paper studies 3DS as a protocol, integration surface, and governance problem, combining standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history, and a bounded live evaluation. We show that client-visible integrations can reflect routing and authentication state before financial authorization, allowing 3DS to function as a profiling and screening channel for issuer controls and cardholder/account state rather than only as a defense. In the tested browser-channel Braintree/Cardinal path, the first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchor cards from bounded adjacent same-range comparison PANs in six of seven distinct ACS/card-range cohorts; separate public evidence, including openly accessible attacker tooling, rotating-proxy support, and illicit paid 3DS card-testing services, shows that comparable signals are already operationalized in the wild. Our live study was deliberately bounded for ethical reasons, so the empirical ceiling reported here reflects researcher restraint rather than an attacker-side scalability limit, although we do not claim network-wide prevalence or candidate issuance. The deeper issue is systemic: decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-boundary assumptions, identifier-linked routing invariants, and fragmented accountability let the exposure persist even when individual actors appear locally conformant. Meaningful remediation therefore requires consortium-level reform, including stricter minimization of client-visible pre-authorization responses, more uniform continuation behavior, and stronger client authenticity and session binding.
author: Wasif Faisal (BRAC University), Suprava Saha Dibya (BRAC University)

title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum
description:
arXiv:2610.32210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Illicit actors exploit Ethereum's deep liquidity and diverse on-chain services to launder criminal proceeds by combining decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers in multi-stage processes. Existing anti-money laundering tracing methods fail to disentangle the underlying asset-flow paths in complex transactions, potentially misdirecting subsequent tracing; cannot identify cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge information; and treat mixers as generic exit services, overlooking post-mixer laundering flows. We present FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets across Ethereum services. First, we propose a method based on the Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to recover intra-transaction asset-flow paths, which guide accurate tracing and service analysis. Second, we extract discriminative features from asset-flow and execution-evidence perspectives and train a classifier to identify transactions with cross-chain intent. Third, we leverage evidence from the upstream laundering network to analyze potential post-mixer laundering activities. Evaluation on 20 real-world laundering cases demonstrates FPTracer's effectiveness. It achieves the highest recall for both known laundering addresses (98.6%) and destinations (94.2%). It identifies all known uses of bridges in these cases and uncovers 30 previously unreported ones. Among 18 cases with identified Tornado Cash usage, FPTracer can identify potential withdrawal-side activities, which are corroborated by public reports where available.
author: Huan Xing, Gaohe Jin, Bang Fu, Yue Li, Baoning Niu, Xing Fan

title: Automated Post-Exploitation Attack Chain Exploration Based on a Phase-guided Hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search Algorithm
description:
arXiv:2610.32278v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advanced attackers in post-exploitation scenarios increasingly craft attack chains that combine benign operations, configuration errors, and vulnerability exploitation to achieve objectives like privilege escalation. While such chains pose significant threats, manually discovering them in complex modern host environments is prohibitively labor-intensive. Automating this discovery is therefore essential for proactive defense, yet existing methods still suffer from inefficiency and lack diversity when exploring these attack chains. To address these limitations, we present APEX, an Automated Post-EXploitation attack chain exploration system. This system transforms attack chain discovery into a planning problem and solves it with a novel phase-guided hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. By organizing attack actions into semantic phases and integrating symbolic planning with MCTS, APEX enables efficient exploration of the state space while generating multiple diverse chains. Evaluations on a benchmark comprising 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems and 291 cloud instances demonstrate that APEX successfully discovers both known and previously unreported attack chains--including 9 novel privilege escalation vectors--providing actionable intelligence for hardening complex production environments.
author: Jie Ying, Mengce Zheng, Ruoxi Chen, Wenrui Cheng, Tiantian Zhu, Zhongjie Zhu

title: Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks on Code Models via Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring
description:
arXiv:2610.32334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pre-trained code models are exposed to backdoor poisoning, in which crafted training samples make the model misbehave on a trigger. A capable attacker minimizes the number of such samples, since each adds cost and exposure and a lower poisoning rate leaves a smaller footprint for defenses. Which samples to poison therefore matters, but existing data-efficient selection methods target image classification, offer no scoring mechanism for autoregressive generation, and have not been studied on code. We propose Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring (TNCS), which isolates a trigger's contribution to the target behavior by comparing the scoring model's output on a triggered input with its output on a trigger-neutralized counterfactual, covering classification and generation alike. TNCS attains higher attack success rates than the baselines at very low poisoning ratios, across three CodeXGLUE tasks and five trigger families, without degrading clean-task performance, and its margin grows as the ratio decreases. It is the only method effective on every trigger family, and its selected poison set transfers to mismatched victims.
author: Yu-Yu Lee, Ming-Feng Tsai, Tomohiro Morikawa, Chun-I Fan

title: Embedding Large PQC KEMs in IKEv2
description:
arXiv:2610.32356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms carry public keys far larger than the established VPN handshake protocol IKEv2 was designed for. At the same time, its initial exchange comprising the public keys cannot be fragmented. In response, the IETF discusses a range of protocol adjustments, yet these proposals have never been compared in terms of their performance and stability under identical conditions. We systematically screened the IETF document corpus for such proposals, added three of our own (one using forward error correction and two using IKEv2 with QUIC, namely QUIKE and QUIKE with a composite key exchange), identified two specification gaps in existing acknowledgment drafts, and implemented all eight on the same open-source codebase. Measurements across different bandwidths, latencies, and packet loss rates, and with ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, and Classic McEliece, total 126 500 handshakes in 1296 different configurations and show that no mechanism fully compensates for the effect of the key size on performance. For Classic McEliece, no approach handles challenging conditions acceptably. The approaches either congest the link or take up to nearly two minutes per handshake on average. For ML-KEM and FrodoKEM, there are two ways forward: building on already standardized extensions or delegating the transport. The former requires the larger implementation change and needs further optimization, such as acknowledgment mechanisms or error-correcting codes, but grants continuity and compatibility. The latter can use a composite key exchange to avoid these drawbacks and achieve a faster, more resilient handshake and leaner implementation, with QUIKE-composite offering the best overall performance.
author: Daniel Herzinger, Marco Thomas, Tobias Handirk, Stefan-Lukas Gazdag, Daniel Loebenberger, Marian Margraf

title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation
description:
arXiv:2610.32453v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.
author: Zifan Peng, Peng Huang, Jingyi Zheng, Yingjie Xue, Xuechao Wang, Xinlei He, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu

title: On Task, Off Track: Benchmarking LLM and Agent Robustness to Near-Target Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.32531v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prompt injection benchmarks assess whether large language models (LLMs) and agents resist malicious instructions embedded in external content. However, a system could perform well by rejecting attacks that obviously abandon the user's request, while still accepting changes that retain most of a legitimate answer but make it incorrect or harmful. Testing more instructions for unrelated outcomes would not necessarily reveal this weakness. We call attacks seeking responses designed to resemble legitimate answers while introducing incorrect or harmful changes near-target prompt injection.
  We introduce NTBench, the Near-Target Benchmark, which builds on legitimate tasks from existing datasets. For each task, a legitimate reference outcome guides the generation of target--instruction pairs, with separate tracks targeting incorrect and harmful outcomes in responses or agent tool invocations. Harmful targets can also accompany otherwise correct task completion. We combine LLM-based checks with human validation of the intended deviations, then assess whether injected instructions induce them using response judgments or tool-call checks, excluding deviations already observed without injection. We evaluate seven LLMs on ten datasets for language tasks and two agent benchmarks. Under a common budget of three attack executions per sample, both tracks achieve higher overall attack success rates than the fixed-target baseline for every evaluated model in each setting. On language tasks, the increases range from 9.3 to 35.8 percentage points for incorrect targets and 1.7 to 17.3 percentage points for harmful targets. These results show that resistance to the tested fixed-target attacks does not imply resistance to related incorrect or harmful outcomes, and that reference-guided targets broaden the failures revealed by robustness evaluation.
author: Yuyang Gong, Zihao Wang, Jiawei Liu, XiaoFeng Wang

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
description:
arXiv:2610.32626v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overhead.
author: Nergiz Yuca, Christian Intern\`o, Nikolay Matyunin, Markus Olhofer, Barbara Hammer, Stefan Katzenbeisser

title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.32661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35-0.93 depending on the type), leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.
author: Amal Neji, Mohamed Fourati, Lamia Chaari Fourati

title: Identity Amortization: Shared Resources and the Cost of Sybil Attacks
description:
arXiv:2610.32685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sybil defenses commonly price identities by requiring a resource for each one. When one resource can support several identities, an adversary can pay less per identity than the defense intends. We call this identity amortization: a strict reduction in the minimum cost of provisioning identities when resources may be shared, relative to provisioning each one independently. It is a second route to the gap that a Sybil attack exploits. When influence is assigned per identity, a defense calibrated to the nominal price can overestimate the cost of a Sybil threshold by up to the number of identities one resource supports. For any resource catalogue, we give exact tests for when identity amortization occurs, where it begins, and its largest error; a sharing cap below the onset removes it. Because the tests need only prices and capacities, they apply to any defense that admits identities against a shareable resource, telling designers whether the assumed per-identity cost is paid, how wrong it can be, and which intervention restores it most cheaply for honest participants. On published phone-verification prices, per-account estimates overstate provisioning cost 1.6 to 4.3 times; Tor's raised per-address relay limit cut modeled attack cost by 8 to 72%, depending on the address-to-relay price ratio.
author: Homayoun Maleki, Nekane Sainz, Jon Legarda, Igor Santos-Grueiro

title: Developing Security Metrics for Automated Compliance Checking
description:
arXiv:2610.32690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To automatically check for compliance with security-related standards, prose requirements must be translated to technical properties to make them measurable. A multitude of metrics have been proposed in past literature, but they are lacking a systematic methodology for their elicitation. Without such a methodology, metrics remain inconsistent in their data models and abstraction levels, they exhibit considerable overlaps and are difficult to combine to comprehensively cover a standard's requirement. In this paper, we develop a data model for security metrics based on a systematization of compliance requirements, and we propose a methodology for their elicitation. The method is based on an ontology that enables a systematic development of metrics with a comparable degree of abstraction. We also present our initial work on an open-source effort that demonstrates that our approach also supports a collaborative development of metrics.
author: Immanuel Kunz, Nico Haas, Angelika Schneider, Christian Banse

title: EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
description:
arXiv:2610.32902v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.
author: Soham Gumaste, Michael Khan, Roland Varriale, Rigel Gjomemo

title: Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.31678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many LLM studies compare how models respond to different follow-up prompts. For example, one prompt may neutrally ask a model to reconsider, while another insists that an invented film really exists. The difference is used to measure the effect of conversational pressure. An automatic scorer then labels whether each response makes an unsupported factual claim. Researchers commonly validate the scorer with one overall accuracy or $F_1$ score. However, high overall performance can hide prompt-specific mistakes: if the scorer makes more errors after one prompt, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction. An audit containing mostly difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive how such errors alter a prompt comparison and examine the problem using six models, 180 invented-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, overall $F_1$ was $.916$. Yet, depending on the prompt, the scorer flagged 2.6%-33.3% of responses that the primary LLM rater judged not to contain an unsupported claim; these prompt-specific estimates were uncertain. In a second audit, the scorer and two separate LLM raters evaluated the same 300 model-question cases under each prompt. An apparent 9.3-point increase from asserting certainty rather than neutrally asking the model to reconsider fell to 2.3 points under both raters. The primary-rater interval included zero, so it did not establish an increase. Two other prompt comparisons kept their direction under both raters, while an attempted prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain for a firm conclusion. Researchers should therefore validate the exact difference they plan to report, not just the scorer as a whole: audit both prompts on matching cases and include scorer and rater uncertainty in the final result.
author: Ancil Crayton

title: MisconceptDialogue: Evaluation Criteria Shape Measured Success in LLM Math Tutoring
description:
arXiv:2610.31679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as math tutors, raising two questions: can a single LLM detect a student's error, diagnose the underlying misconception, and remediate it through multi-turn dialogue - and can we trust the numbers that report how well it does? We address both with MISCONCEPTDIALOGUE, a fully automated framework that runs the full pipeline on five open-weight LLM tutors (7B-14B) interacting with LLM-simulated students over 5,000+ dialogues - a deliberately simulated protocol (paired conditions, a wrong-diagnosis control unsafe with real learners, scale) whose results do not establish real-student learning. On measurement, our headline finding is uncomfortable for the field: benchmark-style exact-match scoring common in standard math NLP - a lower-bound stress test - reports 42.1% measured Remediation Success Rate on identical dialogues where a human-calibrated LLM-as-judge reports 81.3%, a 39.2 percentage-point spread larger than the combined effects of tutor model, teaching strategy, and supplied diagnostic information. This is not a single-judge artifact: four independent LLM judges and 200 human annotations converge to within a few points (kappa up to 0.91). On capability, the verdict is equally striking: the score barely changes whether we tell the tutor the student's actual misconception or a deliberately swapped one - under the tested diagnosis-presentation format, these tutors show little evidence of reliably conditioning on the diagnostic information they are handed. For LLM tutoring evaluation to mature, multi-criterion scoring with multi-judge convergence and human anchoring should become standard practice - and the measurement question deserves as much scrutiny as the capability question it claims to answer.
author: Woojin Lee, Yoonkyu Woo, Jinah Kim, Hyeok-Min Gwon, Jin-Xia Huang

title: Rethinking Structured Generation: Can Graph-Based Reasoning Resolve Ambiguity?
description:
arXiv:2610.31681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured generation is typically formulated as a deterministic mapping from input to a single structured output. This assumption is fundamentally misaligned with natural language, which often admits multiple structurally distinct yet semantically valid interpretations. As a result, existing methods rely on single-reference supervision that collapses ambiguity into one prediction, leading to unstable and inconsistent outputs under underspecified inputs. We reformulate structured generation as an \textit{ambiguity-aware inference problem}, where the objective is to reason over a set of plausible structured outputs rather than predict a single solution. We show that standard training inherently suppresses valid alternatives, and instead adopt a multi-valid learning framework that preserves ambiguity during optimization. To operationalize this formulation, we construct a candidate space of structured outputs, represent each candidate as a graph capturing entities and their relationships, and perform selection via graph-based reasoning over semantic alignment and relational consistency. This enables principled comparison across competing interpretations beyond token-level likelihoods. Experiments on structured generation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, stability, and robustness under varying levels of ambiguity. These results highlight the importance of modeling ambiguity explicitly and suggest a shift from single-output prediction to set-level reasoning in structured generation.
author: Ratun Rahman, Atit Pokharel

title: Multi modal perceived conversation success prediction for spontaneous autistic and non-autistic dyadic interactions
description:
arXiv:2610.31682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversation success is important for communication, social bonds, and well-being and is often reduced in autistic-neurotypical conversations. Previous studies have predicted perceived conversation success using acoustic and lexical features in pediatric autism-enriched samples, or using nonverbal behavior in non-autistic group interactions. Other work has characterized prosodic, facial, motor, and turn-taking synchrony in autistic interactions, but has primarily targeted diagnostic classification or group differences. The present study instead predicts participant perceived conversation success from complementary articulatory, facial, acoustic-prosodic, and turn-taking measures across three spontaneous dyadic-interaction datasets including autistic and non autistic individuals. By leveraging multimodal features, we demonstrate that conversational success is inherently multidimensional and requires a multi-faceted analytical framework. Combining these complementary modalities offers the potential to improve prediction of perceived conversation success by capturing information unavailable from any single modality.
author: Thanushi Withanage, Desi Jones, Noah Sasson, Elizabeth Redcay, Carol Espy-Wilson

title: The Schema Coherence Inventory: Measuring Whether an Assigned Belief Organizes a Language Model's Cognition
description:
arXiv:2610.31683v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Persona-conditioned language models are used as simulated patients and affective agents, but there is no validated way to ask whether a belief assigned to such a model organizes its behaviour or whether the model has merely adopted a mood. We present the Schema Coherence Inventory (SCI): 96 forced-choice items at eight levels of Beck's cognitive model, each offering six replies keyed to three negative self-schemas and their positive counterparts, scored by length-normalized log-likelihood so that nothing is generated or parsed. Affect alone can move a model onto a default belief, so the discriminant criterion is target specificity: a condition built for one belief must select that belief more often than conditions built for the other beliefs of its pole. Six validation studies over 107 conditions on five backbones (1.7B-14B parameters) support this reading. Nine clinically trained raters recover the keyed belief at 79.5% (chance 16.7%). Belief adapters are target-specific on every backbone (+17.7 points; 30/30 belief cells positive), and a condition's SCI profile identifies its own free generations in 24/30 cases against 5 expected by chance. A 48-item short form correlates r = 0.73 with the other 48 items. Applied to six published patient simulators, none carries its formulation's core belief better than a one-sentence statement of it. The validation route, which separates a construct from the affect that accompanies it and checks model judges against clinicians, offers a template for affective measurement in language models; we outline its extension across task types, raters, sites and languages. We release the items, scoring code and short form.
author: Yuqi Wu, Deyang Li, Katharine Hibbard, Ron Oswald, David Sinclair, Adegboyega Sapara, Kalutota Kuruwe Arachchige Sajana Indula Samarasinghe, Abhinav Pillai, Reham Shalaby, Riffat Alam, Xin-Min Li, Yanbo Zhang, Jie Chen

title: Knowledge Graphs Quality Assessment in the Era of LLMs: A Conceptual Framework
description:
arXiv:2610.31684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have been popularized during the last few decades and are increasingly constructed and consumed by Large Language Models (LLMs). Various applications therefore rely on KGs to provide concise, complete, accurate, faithful, fresh, and traceable answers. However, what is the quality of those KGs? In which cases should a KG be used, and can it be trusted to ground an LLM? How might it be evaluated? We reviewed the literature on quality assessment (QA) of data, information, linked data, KGs, and the intersection of KGs and LLMs. We extended the current state-of-the-art frameworks to a catalog of 24 quality dimensions (QDs) and various quality metrics (QMs). Furthermore, we propose a general-purpose, customizable to a domain or task, and practical QA framework for assessing the quality of KGs.
author: Elwin Huaman

title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation
description:
arXiv:2610.31685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
author: Elyas Rashno, Farhana Zulkernine

title: From Target Selection to Condition Reuse: Auditing Residual Interventions in Tool-Use Models
description:
arXiv:2610.31686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation interventions can make a language model produce a target answer, but can the model use the intended condition in other computations? We study this question in Qwen3.5-27B on tool-use tasks where time or permissions determine eligibility and selection. Across 32 fresh worlds, two case-specific residual-writing variants raise familiar target-selection correctness from 35/128 to 119/128 and from 33/128 to 114/128. Yet these gains disappear when familiar facts and identifiers are recombined within the same selection task, while selection of previously rewarded identifiers increases. The gains persist across output formats but yield little improvement in independent judgments about whether a candidate is eligible or should be selected. Internal edits can nevertheless change how a source fact affects a judgment: in a prespecified secondary comparison, an early-layer source patch changes 50/64 judgments when that source is used, with one adverse change among 64 cases where it is not. This selective effect does not ensure correct complete actions. Together, these results separate target-selection control, condition-sensitive judgments, and complete-action correctness. Evaluating how an edited state is used, rather than only its trained answer, exposes these differences.
author: Tianda Sun, Dimitar Kazakov

title: Distributional Alignment of LLMs and Its Generalization Properties
description:
arXiv:2610.31687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate and probe human behavior, e.g., for surveys. For these applications, a key property is that outputs satisfy distributional alignment: to match its output distribution with some reference (in this case, human) distribution. An obstacle in achieving distributional alignment is generalizing from small training data. In this work, we study (1) how to distributionally align LLMs; and (2) how aligned LLMs might generalize to unseen samples and unrelated topics and tasks. Using two large-scale benchmarks, we find that LLMs can indeed achieve distributional alignment and generalize to unseen questions of the same domain. Cross-topic generalization depends on the relationship between topics (e.g., questions about politics are related to trust in institutions). However, aligned LLMs can degrade in surprising ways (e.g., lose their creative ability), suggesting that its generalization properties are inherently unpredictable and unstable.
author: Nelson Jo

title: Tradeoff-Aware Territory Design: A Multi-Objective Decision System for Enterprise Customer-to-Seller Allocation
description:
arXiv:2610.31701v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise customer journeys are shaped not only by product experiences and marketing, but also by recurring resource-allocation decisions. In B2B go-to-market (GTM) organizations, territory carving determines which accounts receive seller coverage, which seller-account relationships are preserved, and how limited field capacity is distributed. Yet the process often remains manual, making it difficult to compare opportunities, value continuity, and evaluate tradeoffs among growth, balance, capacity, and feasibility.
  We present a production decision system for tradeoff-aware customer-to-seller allocation in enterprise GTM planning. It integrates three components: a multidimensional account-value layer that combines predictive signals to score opportunity; an observational continuity-valuation layer that estimates the cost of breaking seller-account relationships using a synthetic-control-style counterfactual framework; and a multi-objective optimization layer that allocates coverage to high-value accounts while considering continuity, opportunity balance, and operational constraints.
  Deployed as a scenario-based decision-support system, the framework enables planners to inspect and compare allocation tradeoffs. Historical backtesting shows that optimizer-generated scenarios substantially improve assignment compliance while maintaining comparable seller-level opportunity distribution. In production planning, adopted scenarios improved both assignment compliance and opportunity balance relative to the previous baseline. Directing scarce seller capacity toward higher-value accounts also offers incremental revenue potential at enterprise scale. The key contribution is an integrated, inspectable framework that turns territory carving into a governable decision process.
author: Nan Wang, Mitchell Turiel

title: LAMB: A Modern Contextual Language Model for Latin
description:
arXiv:2610.31723v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This article introduces Latin Modern BERT (LAMB), an encoder for the Latin language based on the ModernBERT architecture, pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a novel morphologically informed masking regimen. We also present two corpora for the Latin language. Acervus contains 24B BERT WordPiece tokens, including over 760K samples from heavily damaged OCR transcriptions, repaired by a ByT5 model trained for Latin text repair. The second dataset, Corpus Trinum, contains a mixture of over 100M strong and weak Latin language semantic triplets. Corpus Trinum is the first Latin semantic triplet dataset, opening the door for Latin language models to be adapted to general sentence semantic similarity tasks. We construct an experimental grid using five tasks and seventeen subtasks, applying a variety of finetuning configurations and subword aggregation techniques for 15 pretrained encoders, 6 LAMB training checkpoints, and an ablation model designed to quantify the impact of different masking regimens. Using this benchmark, we rank Latin encoders and find that LAMB outperforms all other evaluated models on 16 of 17 subtasks, coming within 0.8 percentage points of state of the art on the seventeenth. We provide additional analyses relating Latin encoder performance to tokenizer behavior, syntactic structure, finetuning configuration, pretraining state, subword aggregation, and variation in source texts and domains. In these, we identify unique acquisition dynamics for Latin open class words during terminal decay phases, and establish that for some task categories, finetuning configuration selection can have a greater effect on downstream scores than additional pretraining tokens.
author: Aidan McCarthy

title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.31789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.
author: Hariharan Devarajan, Neeraj Rajesh, Aniruddha Marathe, Nikoli Dryden, Kin Ng, Michela Taufer

title: Patronizing and Condescending Language Detection in English and Mandarin
description:
arXiv:2610.31808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Patronizing and condescending language (PCL) is a form of harmful language that belittles and assumes pity for vulnerable groups, reinforcing negative societal stereotypes. However, unlike overt hate speech, it is often difficult to detect, even for human judges. This paper proposes a system for the automated detection of PCL. Our first approach uses static word embeddings and a convolutional neural network for classification, while our second approach uses pre-trained BERT embeddings fine-tuned for the PCL task. Our second approach was considerably more successful, and achieved an F1 score of 0.528 over the development set.
author: Xinyi Vicky Xiang, Catherine Qingyun Wang, Paula Cort\'es Lemos

title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
description:
arXiv:2610.31810v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.
author: Jiyuan Tan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Jose Blanchet

title: Free Lunch for LLMs Confidence: The RL Critic Already Knows
description:
arXiv:2610.31820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for trustworthy deployment of large language models (LLMs), but dedicated confidence training stage requires additional data and compute. We ask a fundamental question: what prediction problem does confidence training actually solve? Inspired by prior work on external confidence estimation, we compare self- and external estimators of comparable capacity trained on the same (question, response, correctness) triples. We show that an external model trained solely on a policy's behavioral traces can estimate the policy's confidence as accurately as the policy itself, without accessing the policy's internal representations. This points to a deeper connection with value function learning in reinforcement learning (RL): under a correctness-based outcome, we prove that confidence estimation and critic training are equivalent, both predicting the likelihood that a policy's response will be correct from its trajectory. A simple consequence follows: for LLMs trained with value-based RL, the existing critic can be reused as an off-the-shelf confidence estimator with no additional training or data. The policy remains unchanged, so its task performance is preserved, and the critic provides confidence throughout generation, including intermediate reasoning steps. Across math, code, tool calling, and general reasoning spanning a dozen domains, the reused critic is the best confidence estimator on every in-distribution split and the best-calibrated on 14 of 16, without hurting the task performance.
author: Shujin Wu, Heng Ji

title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
description:
arXiv:2610.31821v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state-of-the-art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment predicts BM25's behaviour, while embedding proximity predicts dense encoders. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known-item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open-weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal-match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what-the-query-remembers.
author: Omar Farouk Zouak, Selma Mani, Larbi Said Chikh, Raid Abderrezak Ouahioune

title: Latent Coherence: Do Frontier Language Models' Probability Judgments Obey the Law of Total Probability?
description:
arXiv:2610.31833v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LawZero's Scientist AI trains a Predictor toward the Bayesian posterior, with an objective that penalizes inconsistent probabilities among latent explanations. We ask whether current frontier language models, with no such training, are already consistent in this sense zero-shot: do their probability judgments satisfy the law of total probability, $P(X)=\sum_z P(z)P(X|z)$, when the latent $z$ must be inferred from records in the context? In separate single-turn calls, models are asked for $P(X)$, for $P(z)$ over the latent's states, and for $P(X|z)$; a causal family applies the same test to $P(y|do(x))$ and the back-door adjustment. Every query has an exact ground-truth probability, and a subset of items is asked in three wordings to separate persistent incoherence from rewording noise. Across seven models, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 are the most coherent (mean absolute residual 0.08 and 0.12 log-odds, about 2 percentage points). Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4-Pro show persistent incoherence (0.27-0.35 log-odds) that is mostly item-specific rather than a shared offset. Within every model, larger residuals go with larger errors against the truth (Spearman 0.40-0.62), so the residual, which needs no ground truth, flags unreliable answers. Reasoning length does not predict coherence, across models or within a model across rewordings of the same question. Simple consistency checks pass almost everywhere; the failures are specific to reasoning through a latent variable. Code and data: https://github.com/ppotash/latent-coherence
author: Peter Potash

title: SAGE: Sense-Aligned Multimodal Grounding Evaluation with Gloss-Augmented Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.31838v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.
author: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu

title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
description:
arXiv:2610.31840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
author: Zihe Song, Wenting Zhao, Ye Liu, Yuanjie Zhu, Ke Xu, Shanghao Li, Philip S. Yu

title: Scaling cross-situational word learning on children's naturalistic experiences
description:
arXiv:2610.31842v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How do children learn the meanings of the simple, concrete words that form a majority of their early vocabulary? Statistical information about many word meanings can be recovered from the gradual accumulation of information about the co-occurrence of words with their referents, a proposal known as ``cross-situational learning''. Contrastive vision--language models allow this learning strategy to be tested on egocentric video data capturing children's early real-life experiences with visual and linguistic inputs. Initial successes of this method on small datasets provide a proof-of-concept, but vision models struggle to learn robust visual representations when trained on these same egocentric videos. How dependent is cross-situational word learning performance on the quality of the model's visual representations? And can cross-situational models scale to larger and more diverse datasets? To address these questions, we trained models on the BabyView corpus, including 2,441 hours of longitudinal egocentric video from 48 children. Models trained on this dataset learned object--label mappings, but performance was far higher when they used internet-pretrained visual representations as opposed to when visual representations were learned solely from the developmental video data. Further, the majority of the learning signal was carried by a small proportion of utterances that described a visible referent. Models learned lexical representations that showed recognizable human-like semantic structure, but model performance showed substantially different trajectories over training experiences than those observed in children. Cross-situational learning is a viable word learning strategy for early noun vocabulary, but constructing developmentally plausible models will require understanding how to learn high-quality visual representations from naturalistic data.
author: Michael C. Frank, Alvin W. M. Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Victor Moreno, Grace Keene-Lee, Meesha R. Ryan, Tarun Sepuri, Jane Yang, Virginia A. Marchman, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Bria Long

title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
description:
arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new
